whyThisMatters: Real fleet decisions are fast — a permit, an invoice, an alert, and you don't always get time to research whether it's genuine. This game trains your reflex for good habits, and helps you catch things that only sound safe.
rememberThis: This month's habit to carry forward: fast instinct is good, but some things only sound safe — a matching PO number, an official-looking notice, a senior title attached to urgency. When you are not sure, slow down and check before you trust the label.

discussionPrompts: Ask the group which bubble tricked them. Most people get at least one of the trick bubbles wrong on their first try.
Ask why a matching PO number on a dry-dock invoice doesn't prove new bank details are genuine.
Ask why a number printed on a port-authority notice might not be trustworthy.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: The most common mistake is tapping anything official-looking — a matching PO number, a senior title, a notice with the right logo — without checking it through the company's own known channel. The trick bubbles are there to catch that habit.

bubbles.text: Verified Vendor Bank Change By Callback
Held Payment To Verify Bank Change
Updated Vendor Bank Details By Email
Paid Port Authority Fee By Email Link

bubbles.note: A second sign-off is a genuinely strong control, but only if that person actually checks the permit rather than approving because a colleague already did.
Matching the PO confirms the invoice is for a real job, but it doesn't by itself prove new bank details are genuine — that still needs a callback.

bubbles.text: Called The Number On The Notice
bubbles.note: A number printed on a suspicious notice may not belong to the real authority — verify through your own known liaison or agent instead.

bubbles.text: Assumed Alert Was Real Because It Looked Right
bubbles.note: An internal tool's look and colours are easy to copy — a genuine alert never asks for your password through a link, however authentic it looks.
